Inside the letters
A deeper look at each: who wrote it and to whom, how it is built, the words it leans on and the Old Testament behind it.
AT A GLANCE
James at a glance
James, all in one place: the letter at a glance, how it is built, the words it leans on and the Old Testament behind it.
VERSES
GREEK WORDS
KEY VERSES
THEMES
THE LETTER

The writer calls himself only "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" and claims no title. Three men of that name appear in the New Testament. James the son of Zebedee was put to death early, which is why most writers rule him out; the views that remain connect the letter with James "the Lord's brother", leader of the church in Jerusalem, though they differ over who he was and whether he wrote it. Mayor noticed wording shared with James's speech and letter in Acts 15: the letter-opening "greeting" appears in the New Testament only here, in the Jerusalem letter of Acts 15:23, and in a Roman officer's letter at Acts 23:26. James 1:1 Acts 12:2 Galatians 1:19 Acts 15:13–23 Acts 23:26 [1][5][8]
KEY VERSES
2My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; 3Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. James 1:2–3 · KJV
Trials as the place where faith learns endurance.
THEMES

Trials and endurance. Testing ripens faith into endurance; "patience" comes three times and "be patient" three more, with the farmer, the prophets and Job held up as patterns. James 1:2–4 James 1:12 James 5:7–11
Wisdom from above. Wisdom is asked of a generous God, and true wisdom is known by a peaceable, gentle life, unlike the jealous "wisdom" from below. James 1:5 James 3:13–18
Hearing and doing. "Doer" comes four times in James; in the rest of the New Testament the word is used only twice. James 1:22–25 James 4:11
Faith shown by works. "Faith" comes 16 times and "works" 15, most of them packed into 2:14–26: faith that does nothing is dead. James 2:14–26
Rich and poor. God has chosen the poor; the rich fade like a flower, and those who hold back wages will answer for it. James 1:9–11 James 2:1–7 James 5:1–6
The tongue. A small member that steers the whole body like a bit or a rudder, and can set a forest alight. James 1:19 James 1:26 James 3:1–12 James 4:11 James 5:12

An undivided heart. "Double minded" (1:8 and 4:8, its only two uses in the New Testament) stands against single loyalty to God; "friendship of the world is enmity with God". James 1:8 James 4:4 James 4:8
Prayer and the Lord's coming. Patience until the Lord comes, prayer in trouble and sickness, and Elijah as proof of what a righteous person's prayer can do. James 5:7–18

A letter of commands. A hand count of the Greek text on this site finds 47 commands in James's own voice in 108 verses (by chapter 11, 4, 4, 12 and 16), plus 7 more inside quoted speech; two of the 47 are "Go to now", which grammarians often treat as an exclamation. This is a hand count, not yet checked against a grammatically tagged Greek text, and other editions of the Greek can add one or two, so published counts vary. The densest runs are 4:7–10, ten commands in four verses, and 5:7–16, thirteen. James 4:7–10 James 5:7–16

Scripture in James. The letter leans on the Old Testament throughout — the "royal law" of loving one's neighbour, Abraham, Rahab, Job, Elijah — but one appeal, "the scripture saith" at 4:5, matches no Old Testament verse. Mayor called it "the difficult passage"; it is left unresolved here. James 2:8 James 4:5 [1]

AT A GLANCE
Peter at a glance
1 Peter and 2 Peter, each in full; then where Peter's readers lived, and the "Babylon" he wrote from.
1 Peter
VERSES
GREEK WORDS
KEY VERSES
THEMES
THE LETTER

"Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ", who also calls himself an elder and a witness of Christ's sufferings. He wrote "by Silvanus" — Paul's companion Silas — and passes on greetings from "Marcus my son", that is John Mark. Eusebius records that the ancient elders used the letter freely as an undisputed work. In modern times Harnack doubted that it came from a personal disciple of Jesus and thought its opening and closing verses were added later; Bigg answered him. 1 Peter 1:1 1 Peter 5:1 1 Peter 5:12–13 Acts 15:40 Acts 12:12 [11][3]
KEY VERSES

3Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, 1 Peter 1:3 · KJV
The opening praise: a living hope through the resurrection.
THEMES

A living hope. In the site's Greek text "hope" appears three times and the verb "to hope" twice; the ISBE calls this the letter of hope. 1 Peter 1:3 1 Peter 1:13 1 Peter 1:21 1 Peter 3:5 1 Peter 3:15 [18]

Suffering. The verb "suffer" comes 12 times and the noun "sufferings" 4: suffering for doing right, as Christ suffered, is the letter's steady subject. 1 Peter 2:19–23 1 Peter 3:14–18 1 Peter 4:1 1 Peter 4:13–19 1 Peter 5:10
Strangers and pilgrims. The readers are sojourners whose true home lies ahead. 1 Peter 1:1 1 Peter 1:17 1 Peter 2:11

Good conduct among outsiders. The word the KJV renders "conversation" — a whole way of life — appears six times, and the words for doing good another six: the answer to slander is a life that silences it. 1 Peter 1:15 1 Peter 2:12 1 Peter 2:15 1 Peter 3:16 1 Peter 4:19

Submission. "Submit" and "be subject" come seven times — to rulers, to masters, wives to husbands, the younger to the elder, and all to one another. 1 Peter 2:13 1 Peter 2:18 1 Peter 3:1 1 Peter 3:5 1 Peter 3:22 1 Peter 5:5
Christ the example and the living stone. "Stone" comes five times in 2:4–8; Christ's suffering is the pattern his people follow. 1 Peter 2:4–8 1 Peter 2:21–24
Grace and glory. "Grace" appears ten times and "glory" eleven — suffering now, glory to follow. 1 Peter 1:11 1 Peter 4:13 1 Peter 5:10

2 Peter
VERSES
GREEK WORDS
KEY VERSES
THEMES
THE LETTER

"Simon Peter, a servant and an apostle of Jesus Christ" — many Greek manuscripts have the Hebrew form "Symeon", used of Peter elsewhere only in James's speech at Acts 15:14. The writer says the Lord has shown him his death is near, that he heard the Father's voice on "the holy mount", that this is his second letter, and he speaks of "our beloved brother Paul". It was the most doubted of the four in the early church, and its authorship is still argued. 2 Peter 1:1 2 Peter 1:14 2 Peter 1:17–18 2 Peter 3:1 2 Peter 3:15–16 Acts 15:14 [3][11][12][13]
KEY VERSES
3According as his divine power hath given unto us all things that pertain unto life and godliness, through the knowledge of him that hath called us to glory and virtue: 2 Peter 1:3 · KJV
God's power has given all that life and godliness need.
THEMES

Knowledge. In the site's Greek text "full knowledge" comes four times and "knowledge" three, and the letter ends "grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord". The ISBE puts it in a line: the key word of 1 Peter is hope, of 2 Peter knowledge. 2 Peter 1:2–8 2 Peter 2:20–21 2 Peter 3:18 [19]

Godliness, and a ladder of virtues. "Godliness" comes four times; to faith the readers are to add virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness and charity. 2 Peter 1:3 2 Peter 1:5–7 2 Peter 3:11
Remembering. The writer means to keep putting them in mind of what they already know, before he is gone. 2 Peter 1:12–15 2 Peter 3:1–2

Judgment kept in store. "Reserved" comes four times and "destruction" or "perdition" six: the angels, the false teachers and the present world are all kept for judgment. 2 Peter 2:4 2 Peter 2:9 2 Peter 2:17 2 Peter 3:7

The Lord's coming. A thousand years are as one day to the Lord; the delay is his patience, and the day of the Lord will come as a thief, bringing new heavens and a new earth. 2 Peter 1:16 2 Peter 3:4 2 Peter 3:8–13
Saviour. The title comes five times, always of Jesus. 2 Peter 1:1 2 Peter 1:11 2 Peter 2:20 2 Peter 3:2 2 Peter 3:18
A rare word. "Cast them down to hell" (2:4) renders a verb meaning "to put in Tartarus", found nowhere else in the Bible; Mayor called it "the extremely rare word". 2 Peter 2:4 [2]

THE WORDS IT LEANS ON
THE OLD TESTAMENT BEHIND IT

2 Peter 3:5–6 quotes Genesis 1:9 Allusion: the earth standing out of the water.
2 Peter 3:5–6 quotes Genesis 7:11 Allusion: the flood.
2 Peter 3:8 quotes Psalms 90:4 Allusion: a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday.

2 Peter 3:13 quotes Isaiah 66:22 Allusion: new heavens and a new earth.
WHERE HIS READERS LIVED

1 Peter names its readers' regions in the order Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia — though Pontus and Bithynia were one Roman province, they stand at opposite ends of the list. Hort took the order to follow the route of the man carrying the letter; Easton thought it the order that would occur to someone writing from Babylon on the Euphrates. Bigg notes that, read loosely, the list covers the whole of Asia Minor except the south coast. Pins mark the site's region centres, not boundaries. 1 Peter 1:1 Acts 2:9 [4][21][3]
WHERE HE WROTE FROM, AND HOW THE LETTER TRAVELLED

Hort argued that the order of the regions in 1 Peter 1:1 is not chance but traces the journey of Silvanus, who carried the letter: landing on the Black Sea coast, going inland through Galatia and Cappadocia, west to Asia, and north to Bithynia to close the circuit. Bigg found the route probable. The towns Hort names are not in the site's place data, so the line joins the region centres and is only a sketch of his route. 1 Peter 1:1 1 Peter 5:12 [4][3]

Where 1 Peter was written depends on what "Babylon" means. These are the two main candidates in the site's place data; a Babylon in Egypt and Jerusalem have also been proposed (see the question on Babylon). 1 Peter 5:13 [10][3][8][18]
AT A GLANCE
Jude at a glance
Jude, all in one place: the letter at a glance, how it is built, the words it leans on and the Old Testament behind it.
VERSES
GREEK WORDS
KEY VERSES
THEMES
THE LETTER

"Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James." He seems to stand apart from the apostles, asking his readers to remember what they foretold. Mayor, Bigg and the ISBE take him to be the brother of Jesus and of James named in Mark 6:3; Easton identifies him with the apostle "Judas of James"; others have proposed a later Judas. Jude 1:1 Jude 1:17 Mark 6:3 Luke 6:16 [2][3][20][21]
KEY VERSES

3Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. Jude 1:3 · KJV
Contend for the faith once delivered to the saints.
THEMES

Things in threes. Mayor noted Jude's fondness for triplets: called, sanctified, preserved; mercy, peace, love; Israel, the angels, Sodom; defile, despise, speak evil; Cain, Balaam, Korah; separating, sensual, without the Spirit. Jude 1:1–2 Jude 1:5–8 Jude 1:11 Jude 1:19 [2]

Kept. "Keep" comes five times. The angels who did not keep their place are kept for judgment, and the intruders are reserved for darkness; the faithful are preserved in Christ and told to keep themselves in God's love. Jude 1:1 Jude 1:6 Jude 1:13 Jude 1:21
Ungodly. The "ungodly" family of words comes six times, four of them inside the prophecy of Enoch. Jude 1:4 Jude 1:15 Jude 1:18
"These are…" Five times Jude points at the intruders with the word "these". Jude 1:8 Jude 1:10 Jude 1:12 Jude 1:16 Jude 1:19

Sources beyond the Old Testament. Jude 14–15 quotes the prophecy of Enoch; R. H. Charles, editing 1 Enoch, judged that the whole of 1 Enoch 1:9 "has been quoted by Jude 14, 15 in a compressed form". Michael's dispute with the devil over the body of Moses (9) is not in the Old Testament; Origen said it came from the "Ascension of Moses", a book whose surviving text no longer contains the scene. Jude 1:9 Jude 1:14–15 [15][16]

Every one of these letters draws on Genesis and Isaiah.

Each line runs from an Old Testament book to the letter that draws on it; its width is the number of passages the letter quotes or clearly alludes to from that book, from the checked lists on this page. Between them the four draw on 69 passages, and only Genesis and Isaiah feed every one. James ranges widest, over twelve books, from the Law and Job to Elijah and Rahab; 1 Peter leans on Isaiah and the Psalms; 2 Peter and Jude both turn to Genesis and Numbers for Sodom and Balaam, 2 Peter adding the flood and Jude adding Cain and Korah. Easton counted about thirty-five Old Testament references in 1 Peter and eleven in 2 Peter, so a fuller list would add fainter allusions. Jude's sources outside the Old Testament, 1 Enoch and the lost Assumption of Moses, are not shown.[21]
